parts.title: How soil microbes and plants work together, and what this tells us about a grassland's recovery over five years
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

Scientists have studied how damaged grasslands recover, looking at the plants, the soil and the microbes living in the soil. Microbes are tiny living things, such as bacteria and fungi. We can map how they are linked to one another as a "microbial network". How this network is connected, and how it relates to plants, gives important clues about how far a grassland has recovered. Still, we do not yet know how the microbial network affects the way plants and microbes interact, or how it reflects recovery, at different stages of a grassland's recovery.

Methods

We followed a grassland for 5 years as it recovered. We compared four stages: early, moderate and late recovery, and a final stage where the plant community is stable. At each stage we looked at how the soil microbial networks, the amount of plant material and the soil's properties changed. We worked out a score called the grassland restoration index (GRI) to judge how far each site had recovered. We also built microbial co-occurrence networks, which are maps of which microbes tend to rise and fall together, to see how the microbial communities changed over the 5 years.

Results

In the early recovery stage, the main plant changed from Kochia sieversiana to Chloris virgata. The complexity of the bacterial network went up and down over the 5 years, which points to recovery in the early stage. In the moderate and late stages, the bacterial networks became gradually more complex, which suggests that these grasslands have a growing ability to recover. However, the GRI score showed that the moderate and late stages did not move on to the next stage of recovery over the 5 years. We also used a computer method called random forest regression, which tests many possible factors to find which ones best predict an outcome. It showed that high soil pH may hold back recovery by shaping the soil microbial networks. (Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, and a high pH means alkaline soil.)

Conclusion

Our study sheds light on the role soil microbial networks play as signals during recovery. It suggests that grasslands in the moderate and late stages may take longer to reach a stable community. We stress that soil pH may be a key limit on recovery at the different stages, and that future experiments should test whether adjusting soil pH can help recovery.

Keywords: grassland, how microbes and plants interact, microbial network, recovery process, soil properties
parts.introduction_first:
Human activities and climate change have damaged grasslands to different degrees (Gao et al., 2025). Today, people use several methods to bring back the plants and soil of damaged grasslands, such as putting up fences and growing plants for grazing animals (Cao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2018). When it comes to plants, the goal is to help them grow more and to bring back the plants that naturally belong in the area (Jing et al., 2015). When it comes to soil, the goal is to rebuild the community of microbes living there. This is harder, and it decides how the grassland's recovery unfolds over time (Liu et al., 2019).

In recent years, many studies have found that some grasslands stay stuck at a certain stage of recovery and struggle to return to their undamaged state (Kardol and Wardle, 2010). An idea called the theory of multiple stable states says that a grassland can settle into more than one lasting condition. It suggests that grasslands may have natural limits to their recovery, set by their soil (Liu M. et al., 2025; Chaparro-Pedraza, 2024). These limits affect how well plants grow by shaping the microbial community, and so they hold back the recovery of the grassland (Liu M. et al., 2025). This means that changes in the make-up of the soil microbial community are the key to understanding how a grassland recovers. Yet scientists have only recently begun to recognize how important these changes in microbes are for grassland recovery.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

We studied short-term grassland recovery at different stages by following how the microbial community changed. In the early recovery stage, the bacterial network went up and down over 5 years, and the main plant changed from K. sieversiana to C. virgata. In the moderate and late stages, the microbial networks became more complex, which showed that these grasslands have the potential to recover. Even so, these stages showed no sign of moving on to the next stage of recovery over the 5 years.

We also found that high soil pH might limit how complex the bacterial network becomes and slow down recovery. However, plants and microbes may take a long time to bring soil pH back to normal on their own. We need an experiment that actively changes the soil pH to check how lowering it affects the grassland's recovery.

Overall, our study gives evidence that the structure of the microbial network reflects how a grassland is recovering. It stresses that adjusting soil pH by hand may be a key way to help grasslands recover.
parts.introduction_rest:
Grassland recovery means that the soil and the plant community of a grassland get back to health. This can happen when people step in to help, or when nature does it on its own (Bardgett et al., 2021). The final goal is to bring the plants and soil of a damaged grassland back to the condition they had before the damage (Sun et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2010). Because plants and soil change in different ways as recovery goes on, scientists sort grassland recovery into three stages: early, moderate and late (Liu et al., 2021; Liu M. et al., 2025; Pellant et al., 2005).

In the late stage, the plants and soil are close to those of an undamaged grassland (Su and Zhang, 2004). The moderate stage has a high variety of plants, and it marks the dividing line between recovery that succeeds and recovery that does not (Liu et al., 2021). In the early stage, the plant community and the soil are badly damaged, so the grassland finds it hard to recover by itself (Dong et al., 2011). For example, putting up fences and banning grazing works well to bring back the plant community in the moderate and late stages (Sun et al., 2020). In the early stage, people need to grow plants for grazing animals and improve the soil so that recovery goes faster (Feng et al., 2010).

However, earlier studies have shown that a plant community during recovery may struggle to move on to the next stage (Hu et al., 2016; Li et al., 2023). This may be because grassland soil is very uneven, so its nutrients are spread out unevenly (Gao et al., 2019). As a result, the nutrient-rich spots grow patches of different plant communities, while some areas stay at the same stage of recovery (Jiang et al., 2010). Uneven soil often comes with high soil pH and salty soil, and these made grasslands break up into smaller, separated pieces and slowed down recovery (Liu et al., 2021). For all these reasons, scientists still disagree strongly about how damaged grasslands recover, and how well, in soils of different kinds.

Soil microbes play a key part in many natural processes, such as recycling nutrients and the way plant communities change over time (Breidenbach et al., 2022). Microbes react quickly to changes in their surroundings and in the plants around them, so the make-up of the microbial community usually shifts as a grassland recovers (Li et al., 2016; Akiyama and Kawamura, 2007). This means that changes in the microbial community are an important sign of how far recovery has gone (Fry et al., 2017).

In recent years, many studies have looked at these changes using microbial networks (Guseva et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2023). A microbial network is complicated, and it shows how microbes respond to living and non-living factors through the links between them (Xue et al., 2022). So the complexity of the microbial network may change as a grassland recovers (Ding et al., 2023; Morrien et al., 2017). In general, a more complex microbial network means the soil is doing more jobs well, which suggests the grassland has the potential to recover (Chen et al., 2022; Du et al., 2025; Mi et al., 2026).

However, microbial networks are closely tied to the make-up of the plant community (Finck et al., 2026). As a grassland recovers, both its plants and its soil change, and this may bring matching changes in the microbial networks (Jayaramaiah et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025). For example, the moderate stage usually has more kinds of plants than the late stage (Liu et al., 2021), which may lead to a more complex microbial network in the moderate stage. So it is still unclear how the complexity of the microbial network changes from one stage of recovery to another.

Soil microbes drive the recovery of grasslands through the way they interact with plants (Lozano et al., 2014). Helpful interactions between microbes and plants push recovery forward when soil conditions are harsh (Pii et al., 2015). But as the soil improves and more nutrients become available, these helpful interactions may give the most common plants an edge over the others and slow down recovery (Guo et al., 2019). For instance, in the early stage the soil has few nutrients, which holds back plant growth. Helpful interactions between microbes and plants can help plants take up nutrients more efficiently and help the grassland recover (Brzostek et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2019). As a grassland recovers, plants use these helpful interactions to strengthen their edge, which makes it harder for other plants to take over and so holds back recovery (Li et al., 2019).

However, the theory of multiple stable states suggests that soil conditions at different stages of recovery affect how microbes and plants interact, so recovery works better in some cases than in others (Liu M. et al., 2025). For example, a grassland that is only lightly damaged can quickly return to the condition it had before the damage (Dong et al., 2020). This is because the plants and soil were hardly harmed, so the plants can quickly build helpful interactions with soil microbes and return to an undamaged state (Sun et al., 2020; Gann et al., 2019). In contrast, the early stage of a badly damaged grassland may last a long time. Sowing new plants for grazing animals can bring back the amount of plant material, but the harsh soil makes it hard for microbes and plants to form helpful interactions (Dong et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2021). Overall, scientists still debate a great deal about how damaged grasslands recover. Whatever theory we use, making clear how the interactions between microbes and plants change is key to understanding how grassland recovery unfolds and which way it goes.

In this study, we set out to find how the make-up of the microbial community and its networks affect recovery at different stages. We followed a grassland as it recovered naturally for 5 years. During that time we made three field visits to measure the plants, the soil and the microbial communities at different stages of recovery: early, moderate and late, and a final stage where the community is stable. Earlier studies suggest that the microbial network becomes more complex as soil conditions improve and the plant community recovers (Mi et al., 2026). At the same time, high soil pH is a typical feature of damaged grasslands in this area (Liu et al., 2021), and recovery can strengthen the interactions between plants and microbes (Lozano et al., 2014; Kardol and Wardle, 2010). We therefore made two predictions. First, we expected that the microbial network would become more complex as recovery went on, which would raise the grassland's potential to recover. Second, we expected that microbial networks would steer the recovery process through the interactions between microbes and plants, and that high soil pH might be a key limit on grassland recovery.
parts.methods:
Materials and methods

### Where we did the study

We carried out this study at the Tongyu Semi-Arid Climate-Environment Field Station (122°52′E, 44°25′N), on the Songnen Plain in northeastern China. The station covers 47.7 hm2 (hectares) of meadow steppe, a type of grassland with a mix of grasses and flowering plants. Its most common plant is Leymus chinensis, a grass. On average, 404 mm of rain and snow falls each year, and 80% of that falls between May and September. The average yearly temperature is 5.7 °C. The coldest month is December, when it drops to −32 °C, and the warmest is June, when it reaches 39 °C. The soil varies a great deal from place to place. It includes sandy soils, slightly chernozem soils (a dark, rich soil type), salty soils, alkaline soils and meadow soils (Gao et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021).

Since 2006, fences have kept grazing animals out of this meadow steppe. Before the fences went up, the area had been grazed at different strengths, and this had damaged the grassland (Wang and Ripley, 1997; Jiang et al., 2010). Because of this, the grasslands here are damaged to different degrees, depending on how heavily they were grazed. Heavy grazing happened around water sources. From 2006 to 2021, some of the damaged sites slowly recovered. However, the soil in this area holds few nutrients and is very salty, and this holds back the recovery of damaged grasslands (Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024). For these reasons, many of the restored sites have stayed at the stage where they were restored.

Following earlier studies and the official guidelines for judging grassland damage and recovery, we sorted the area into four stages: early, moderate and late recovery, and a final stage where the plant community is stable (a stable L. chinensis community) (Su and Zhang, 2004; Pellant et al., 2005). We also worked out the grassland restoration index (GRI) score to check how far each site had recovered, using this equation:

GRI = 13(13P1 − 13P2 − 13P3) + 13(13TC + 13TN + 13TP) + 13(12SW − 12pH)

Here, P1, P2 and P3 are the relative abundances of three groups of plants. Relative abundance means how common a plant is compared with all the plants in the area. P1 is the climax species, the plant that belongs in a fully mature, undamaged grassland. P2 is annual species, plants that live for only one year. P3 is salinization indicator species, plants that signal salty soil. TC, TN and TP are the relative amounts of total carbon (C), nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) in the soil. SW is the relative soil water content, measured by weight, and pH is the soil pH. To get each relative value, we divided that factor's value by the sum of that factor across all four stages of recovery.

Earlier work has shown that the GRI score can tell apart the different stages of recovery in the meadow steppe of the Songnen Plain (Zeng et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). We treat the GRI score of the stable stage as 100% of the recovery level. Scores below 55% mean early recovery, scores from 55% to 80% mean moderate recovery, and scores from 80% to 90% mean late recovery. These cut-off points come from an earlier study near the Tongyu station (Yang et al., 2021), and our own field survey confirmed that they are accurate (Table 1).

### Surveying the plants and collecting the soil

In August 2021, we picked four plots at random in each stage of recovery (ND, LD, MD and SD). To keep differences in the surroundings as small as possible, each 10 m × 10 m plot held plots from all four stages. The plots were at least 200 m apart, so that each soil sample would fairly represent its area. Inside each plot, we picked one 1 m × 1 m square, called a quadrat, at random for collecting plants and soil. Earlier studies show that this size of sampling site is a reasonable way to capture what the wider area is like (Zeng et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021). In each quadrat, we cut all the plants and measured the aboveground biomass of each plant species, meaning the weight of the plant parts above the soil. We collected and measured the plants in the same way as an earlier study at the Tongyu station (Zhang et al., 2024). In August 2023 and 2025, we picked a new 1 m × 1 m quadrat at random close to the 2021 quadrat. We collected plants and soil in the same way as in 2021.

Next, we collected soil at the same plant survey sites. After clearing away fallen leaves and other dead plant material, we used a soil auger (a 4 cm wide tool that drills into the ground) to take 1 kg of fresh soil from the top 0 to 15 cm. We took soil 4 times at random in each quadrat and mixed it into one soil sample for each plot (4 kg). We passed these soils through a sieve with 2 mm holes and split each one into two parts. We let one part dry in the air and used it to measure the soil's properties: its carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus, its pH, and its water content by weight. We froze the other part straight away in liquid nitrogen and took it to the laboratory to study the bacteria and fungi.

### Measuring the plant and soil samples

To measure the amount of plant material, we first heated each plant sample at 105 °C for 15 minutes and then at 65 °C for 48 hours, which dried it. To study the soil bacteria and fungi, we used high-throughput sequencing, a method that reads the DNA of many microbes at once. We pulled the DNA out of the soil using the MoBio PowersoilTM DNA Isolation Kits (MoBio Laboratories, Inc., USA).

To find out which bacteria and fungi were present, we copied one particular stretch of their DNA many times over. Short pieces of DNA called primers mark where the copying starts and stops. For bacteria, we copied the V3–V4 regions of the rRNA gene using the primers F: 5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA-3′ and R: 5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′. For fungi, we copied the ITS1 region of the rRNA gene using the primers F: 5′-CTTGGTCATTTAGAGGAAGTAA-3′ and R: 5′-GCTGCGTTCTTCATCGATGC-3′. Genesky Biotechnologies Inc. (Shanghai, China) then read the copied DNA from both ends on an Illumina MiSeq machine. The Supplementary material gives the full details of how we extracted the soil DNA and sequenced it.

After checking the quality of the data, we kept 3179 bacterial and 2264 fungal operational taxonomic units (OTUs). An OTU is a group of DNA sequences that are at least 97% identical, and we treat each one as a kind of microbe. The data also held 79875 clean reads for bacteria and 79761 for fungi on average. The data are stored in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database under the number PRJNA1475409.

To measure the soil's water content by weight, we dried the samples at 105 °C until their weight stopped changing. Once the soil was dry, we measured its total carbon with a total organic carbon analyzer (Vario TOC, Elementar, Germany), its total nitrogen with a Kjeldahl apparatus (Kjeltec 8,400, FOSS, Denmark), and its total phosphorus with an automatic discontinuous chemical analyzer (Smartchem 450, AMS, Italy). To measure soil pH, we mixed soil with water (5 parts water to 1 part soil) and tested the mixture with a pH meter (pH S-3C, INESA, China).

### How we analysed the data

We used a test called one-way ANOVA to check whether the year of sampling affected the amount of plant material and the soil properties at the different stages of recovery. ANOVA compares the averages of several groups and asks whether the differences between them are bigger than chance alone would usually produce. We also used one-way ANOVA to test how the alpha diversity of bacteria and fungi changed across the different years. Alpha diversity describes the variety of microbes within a single sample. To see how the different years affected the beta diversity of the microbes, we used a method called Nonmetric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS). Beta diversity describes how different the microbial communities are from one sample to another. NMDS draws these differences as a map, where samples with similar communities sit close together.

We used co-occurrence networks to find the built-in links within the microbial communities and the links between the microbes and the plants. We built these networks at the level of species. We included only microbes whose average abundance was more than 0.1%, so that the Spearman correlations would be accurate. We ran the analysis in the R program and worked out the features of each network's shape with the "igraph" package (Lupatini et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2018).

To draw the links in the network, we calculated Spearman rank correlations between every possible pair of microbial species. A Spearman correlation measures how closely two things rise and fall together, from −1 to 1. Using the "psych" and "multtest" packages, we counted a link as a real co-occurrence only when the correlation, ρ, was above 0.6. Because we tested so many pairs, some would pass this bar by chance alone. So we adjusted all the P-values (P < 0.01) using the false discovery rate (FDR) method, which keeps down the number of such false alarms (Benjamini et al., 2006).

In these networks, each point, or node, stands for a kind of bacterium or fungus (at the species level), and each line, or link, stands for a statistically significant correlation between two kinds. We got these microbes after first removing low-quality reads (a quality score below 20 or sequences shorter than 100 bp, the letters of DNA). We then grouped sequences that were at least 97% identical using the UPARSE pipeline, a set of computer steps for sorting DNA sequences. We removed any groups that held only one sequence. We named each OTU using the RDP Classifier, a tool that matches DNA sequences to known microbes.

We built and analysed the networks in the program Gephi (0.9.2). We also ran a robustness analysis to check how stable each co-occurrence network was. The network features we measured were the number of nodes and links, the clustering coefficient (how often a node's neighbours are also linked to each other), the average degree (how many links each node has on average), the average path length (how many steps it takes to get from one node to another), the modularity (how much the network splits into separate clusters) and the graph density (how many of all possible links are present).

To compare our networks with chance, we built a random network (an Erdös-Rényi network) with the same number of nodes and links as the real network, using the subnet_property function of the "meconetcomp" package. We made these random networks by taking the full network and keeping only the OTUs found in one sample, along with the links between them. We then measured the shape of each of these smaller networks. We used these features, across the different stages and years, to study how the year of recovery and the soil's properties affected how complex the microbial networks were.

We also built a network of links between the microbial communities and the different plant species. We built it in the same way as the co-occurrence networks, using Spearman's correlation with ρ above 0.6 and P below 0.01.

To find out how much the soil's properties mattered for how complex the microbial networks were, we used the "randomForest" and "A3" packages to build a random forest regression model. We also checked how the soil's properties were correlated with network complexity using Pearson correlation, another way of measuring how closely two things rise and fall together. We did all the statistical analyses in R 4.0.2 (R Core Team, 2015).
parts.results:
Results

### Plants and soil over the 5 years of recovery

In the early recovery stage, the total amount of plant material slowly rose over the five years, and so did the amount of C. virgata. Over the same years, the amount of K. sieversiana slowly fell.

The moderate recovery stage was marked by L. chinensis together with forbs, which are small flowering plants that are not grasses. This stage had a high variety of plants, and L. chinensis was the main plant. In the late recovery stage, the plants were L. chinensis, L. daurica and Carex duriuscula. The amount of L. chinensis was significantly higher in this stage than in the early and moderate stages. L. chinensis reached its highest amount in the stage where the plant community is stable.

Over the five years, the total amount of plant material did not increase significantly in the moderate, late or stable stages (Table 1).

The soil changed in different ways at each stage. In the early recovery stage, the soil's total nitrogen and total phosphorus rose significantly over the 5 years. In the moderate stage, total phosphorus in 2023 was significantly higher than in the other years, and soil pH fell significantly in 2025. In the stable stage, total phosphorus in 2025 was significantly lower than in the other years. Across all four stages, the soil held the most water in 2025 and the least in 2023 (Table 2).

### Variety of soil microbes and how they are linked

To measure how varied the microbes were, we used the Shannon index. This score goes up when there are more kinds of microbes and when they are spread more evenly. Over the 5 years, the bacterial Shannon index went up and down: in most stages it first fell and then rose. The fungal Shannon index, however, did not change significantly between the years (Figure 1).

We also compared how different the microbial communities were from one year to another, using a method called nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS). It draws a kind of map where samples with similar communities sit close together. This showed that the difference between years in the make-up of the bacterial and fungal communities was not significant (Figure 2).

FIGURE 1

Bacterial (a,c,e,g) and fungal (b,d,f,h) Shannon index in the three years of recovery. Bars show the average ± standard error of 4 samples. Different letters show a statistically significant difference (P < 0.05) between the 3 years.

FIGURE 2

NMDS maps of the make-up of the soil bacterial (a,c,e,g) and fungal (b,d,f,h) communities at the different stages of recovery. Each colour shows how the community changed in a different year. The colours are based on the Bray-Curtis distance, a measure of how different two communities are, and the 95% confidence intervals show the uncertainty around them.

Next, we looked at how complex and stable each microbial network was. A network is more complex when its members are linked to more others. It is more stable when it keeps working even when some members are lost. Over the five years, the bacterial networks became gradually more complex and stable (Figures 3a–c,g). The fungal networks went up and down (Figures 3d–f,h).

We then looked at smaller groups within each network, called sub-networks. For each sample, we used the number of links each member had to these sub-networks as a measure of how complex the network was. In the early recovery stage, the complexity of the bacterial network went up and down. In the other stages, it rose gradually (Figures 4a–d). The fungal network behaved differently. Its complexity fell gradually in the early and moderate stages, but rose gradually in the late stage and in the stable stage (Figures 4e–h).

FIGURE 3

Microbial networks (a–f) and their stability (g,h) in different years, built at the level of species. Each dot is one bacterial phylotype, a type of bacterium identified at the species level. Each colour marks a separate module, a tight cluster of dots found with the modularity tool in the Gephi software using its default settings. Dots in the same module may do similar jobs and share the same place in the ecosystem. The different colours show how the microbes divide up their roles across the network, and they partly predict how the network's shape relates to different soil jobs. A line joins two dots only when they are strongly linked (Spearman's ρ > 0.6) and the link is statistically significant (P < 0.01). Spearman's ρ measures how closely two things rise and fall together. Bigger dots have more links. The stability test shows how the network's natural connectivity changes as dots are removed one by one. A bigger change for the same number of removed dots means the network is less stable and less robust.

FIGURE 4

The number of links in the sub-networks of bacteria (a–d) and fungi (e–h) at the different stages of recovery. Bars show the average number of links for each stage (4 samples). The sub-networks were taken from the bacterial and fungal networks.

### How plants and microbes are linked, and what affects the networks

Our network analysis showed that the links between plants and microbes grew stronger over the years of recovery. L. chinensis, C. duriuscula and L. daurica were positively linked with the bacterial network, meaning they tended to rise and fall together, and these links grew gradually over the 5 years. C. virgata, K. sieversiana and A. scoparia were negatively linked with the bacterial network (Figure 5).

Over the five years, the positive links with the fungal network grew gradually for L. chinensis but shrank for C. duriuscula. C. virgata and K. sieversiana were negatively linked with the fungal network (Figure 6).

FIGURE 5

Links between the soil bacterial network (at the species level) and the amount of each plant in different years. Blue lines show positive links and red lines show negative links between the microbes and the amount of plant material (Spearman's ρ < 0.6, P < 0.01). The dots are coloured by phylum, a broad group of related microbes.

FIGURE 6

Links between the soil fungal network (at the species level) and the amount of each plant in different years. Blue lines show positive links and red lines show negative links between the microbes and the amount of plant material (Spearman's ρ < 0.6, P < 0.01). The dots are coloured by phylum.

The random forest regression showed that soil pH is the main factor affecting the bacterial and fungal networks (Figures 7a,b). We also used Pearson correlation, which measures how closely two things rise and fall together. It showed that the soil's total carbon and total nitrogen were positively linked with how complex the microbial networks were, while soil pH was negatively linked with it. The complexity of the bacterial network was also positively linked with soil water content (Figure 7c).

FIGURE 7

The random forest regression (a,b) and Pearson correlation (c) show which soil properties mainly drive the number of links in the bacterial and fungal networks. For the random forest, we worked out how much each soil property mattered to the model's accuracy, tree by tree, and then averaged this over all 5000 trees. The measure is based on how much the model's mean squared error (MSE), a measure of its prediction mistakes, goes up. In (a,b), a bar marked * (P < 0.05) means that soil property has a statistically significant effect on the number of links in the microbial network. In (c), blue squares show positive links and red squares show negative links between soil properties and the number of links. ***, P < 0.001; **, P < 0.01; *, P < 0.05. TC, total carbon; TN, total nitrogen; TP, total phosphorus; pH, soil pH; SW, soil water content.

Discussion

How plants and soil changed at each stage of recovery

Over the 5 years, the amount of plant material rose significantly only in the early recovery stage. (We call a rise "statistically significant" when a rise this large would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no change.) In that stage, the main plant also changed to C. virgata (Table 1). These results show that the early stage was on the way to recovery over this short period. However, this recovery does not mean that the early stage can go on to return to the undamaged state (Sun et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). The soil's properties and the nutrients it holds are still the main things holding back recovery in the early stage (Li et al., 2023). The change in the main plant may be because C. virgata competes better than K. sieversiana for light and soil nutrients (Zhou et al., 2019; Hautier et al., 2009; Li et al., 2020).

Our results also showed that the plants in the moderate stage need more time to recover, which matches an earlier study (Liu M. et al., 2025). This may be because the soil recovers slowly, and soil in the moderate stage may take more than 10 years to recover (Bai et al., 2020). Our results also suggested that the plant community in the late stage cannot become stable in the short term. The reason may be that the soil in the Songnen grassland varies a great deal from place to place (Gao et al., 2019). This patchiness may mean that the amount of nutrients in the soil differs between different parts of the Songnen grassland (Liu et al., 2021). In some areas, the plant communities may be held back more strongly by a lack of soil nutrients. When a grassland is recovering, a severe shortage of soil nutrients may make the soil environment harder to recover, so recovery takes longer.

We found that the total amounts of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) in the soil slowly rose in the early stage, but went up and down from year to year in the moderate and late stages (Table 2). These results suggest that the soil in the early stage may be recovering. There are two possible reasons. First, the fences help plants grow and stop the soil from being packed down. This lets more nitrogen stay in the soil, because less of it is lost to the air through a process called denitrification (Dong et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2020). Second, as the total amount of plant material grows, more organic matter (material from dead plants and animals) builds up in the soil (Liu et al., 2016). Microbes break this organic matter down, which may raise the total nitrogen and phosphorus in the soil (Wallenstein and Burns, 2011).

Even so, compared with the stable stage, the early stage still had low soil nutrients and a high pH (Table 2). So the soil in the early stage still needs a longer time to recover (Sun et al., 2020). In the moderate and late stages, the amount of water in the soil may explain why total phosphorus went up and down across the years. The soils of the Songnen grassland are very salty and alkaline, so they hold on to water strongly (Zeng et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019). As a result, in wetter years, more rain makes the soil wetter, more water washes nutrients out of the soil, and the soil ends up with less phosphorus (Mi et al., 2025).

How soil microbes changed over the five years of recovery

We first looked at alpha diversity, which describes how many kinds of microbes live in one place and how evenly they are spread. Over the 5 years, the variety of bacteria was more sensitive to change than the variety of fungi (Figure 1). This may be because the soil environment in a damaged grassland affects bacteria and fungi in different ways. In particular, the high soil pH caused by grassland damage can hold back fungi but boost bacteria (Rousk et al., 2010). This makes the bacterial community respond more strongly to changes in the soil.

As a grassland recovers, the number and variety of bacteria are generally linked to conditions such as soil nutrients and moisture, while fungi are linked to which plants are growing (Dong et al., 2021; Cuartero et al., 2024). So the variety of fungi stayed steady across the different stages of recovery, perhaps because the mix of plants did not change much. Meanwhile, the variety of bacteria may have changed because of the soil's properties, especially changes in soil moisture over the 5 years (Liu B. et al., 2025).

We also looked at beta diversity, which describes how different the microbial communities are from one place to another. It showed no statistically significant differences over the 5 years (Figure 2). This means we could not show a change, though it does not prove there was none. The finding suggests that the make-up of the microbial community stayed stable across the different stages of damage during the 5 years of recovery (Guo et al., 2019). In undamaged grasslands, a stable microbial community strengthens helpful links between the most common species and microbes (Hou et al., 2023), which helps plants grow. During recovery, a stable microbial community suggests that the recovery process may stay steady over the short term (Du et al., 2025). Microbes and plants may be building up the potential to recover, but this did not cause a significant shift to the next stage of recovery.

The microbial networks suggested that the number of kinds of bacteria may slowly rise and form more complex communities over the 5 years (Figure 3). A growingly complex microbial network may point to a grassland's potential to recover (Mi et al., 2026). However, damaged grasslands recover slowly. This may be because soil pH falls gradually and nutrients build up, which takes more than 10 years (Feng et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2020). So the soil microbes are shaped by this slow recovery and by long-term conditions in similar soils (Jiang et al., 2010), which may lead to stable community make-ups (Yan et al., 2025).

Interestingly, the complexity of the bacterial network in the early stage went up and down (Figure 4a). This may be because the growth of pioneer species, the first plants to move into a damaged area, improves the soil (Jing et al., 2015). Soil nitrogen and phosphorus rose significantly over the 5 years, which kept shifting the bacterial communities (Liu et al., 2020; Mi et al., 2025) and so made the bacterial network less complex. The complexity of the fungal network also slowly fell in the early and moderate stages (Figures 4e,f). This may be because the high soil pH and harsh conditions in these stages can limit how well fungi grow and how many kinds there are (Rousk et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, the complexity of both the bacterial and fungal networks rose in the late stage (Figures 4c,g). This suggests that the late stage is on the way to the stable stage. However, moving from one stage of recovery to the next often involves changes in which plants grow and in what the soil does, and these can bring matching changes in the microbial networks (Jayaramaiah et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025). In general, how complex a microbial network is is closely linked to how many kinds of plants there are (Finck et al., 2026). On the Songnen Plain, the late stage has more kinds of plants than the stable stage (Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024), which may encourage a more complex microbial network in the late stage. So the move from the late stage to the stable stage is likely to involve ups and downs in the microbial networks, and 5 years of recovery is not long enough to cause such a change.

The key factor affecting the microbial network and grassland recovery

The network of links between plants and microbes showed that the plant L. chinensis became more and more closely linked to the microbial communities over the 5 years (Figures 5, 6). This points to a positive effect on grassland recovery during the 5 years. L. chinensis copes well with drought, high soil pH and poor soil (Wang et al., 2004). Because of this, it is a pioneer species in grassland recovery and one of the most common plants in local grasslands (Liu et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2018). So the growing positive links between L. chinensis and microbes suggest that L. chinensis is building up an advantage over its competitors as the grassland recovers. However, the results for the amount of L. chinensis and for the complexity of the microbial network also showed that the grasslands in the moderate and late stages stayed at their stage of recovery.

We also found that most microbes were negatively linked with C. virgata and K. scoparia (Figures 5, 6). This means that when these plants were more common, those microbes tended to be less common. In harsh conditions, C. virgata and K. scoparia can grow quickly and cope well with salty, alkaline soil (Lin et al., 2015). These traits make them the most common plants in the early stages of recovery (Hautier et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2019). As recovery goes on, plants that live for only one year are gradually replaced by plants that live for many years and use nutrients more efficiently (Kardol et al., 2006). The helpful links between long-lived plants (such as L. chinensis) and microbes weaken the competitive advantage of C. virgata and K. scoparia (Li et al., 2024; Dangi et al., 2024), so their negative links with microbes grow.

We found that high pH is the main factor limiting how complex the microbial network becomes (Figure 7). The soil pH in this area is high because the soil of the damaged grassland is very salty (Singh, 2015; Jiang et al., 2010). There are three steps to this. First, the alkaline salts that make the soil salty come from climate change and from the rock and soil material the soil formed from (Wang L. et al., 2009). In undamaged grassland, rain dissolves these salts, and they wash down into the groundwater through the larger gaps in the soil (Wang and Ba, 2008). Second, as the soil gets packed down, these larger gaps are destroyed. Salts then keep building up at the surface, which creates the high soil pH typical of this area (Steffens et al., 2008). Finally, during grassland recovery, high soil pH can upset the balance of nutrients in the soil (Jiao et al., 2016; Mitsuta et al., 2025). When the soil's structure gets worse, microbes and plants cannot grow normally (Wang Z. et al., 2009), which holds back the grassland's recovery.

However, our results showed that soil pH fell only in the moderate stage. This may be because plants and microbes change soil pH only slowly (Sun et al., 2020; Liu M. et al., 2025). So these grasslands have a strong potential to recover, but they stayed at their stage of recovery throughout the 5 years. High soil pH may be one of the key factors holding back recovery.

The study area also has very salty soil, and high soil pH is its most typical feature. Earlier studies have shown that in this region, salty soil affects microbial communities mainly through soil pH (Bai et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024). However, we did not directly measure how salty soil affects the microbial networks. Instead, we worked out the role of soil pH in these networks mainly from the random forest regression computer method. So it is necessary to run experiments that change soil pH and saltiness on purpose to see how they affect recovery.

The main aim of our study was to find out how microbial networks changed over a 5-year recovery period in the "recovery series": the early, moderate and late stages, and the stable L. chinensis community. To do this, we built the microbial networks using data from the same year, so that we could see the overall trend of how the networks changed across the whole recovery series over the 5 years. We chose our sample plots so that the outside conditions were as similar as possible. Even so, there were still unavoidable differences between the stages of recovery and between the sampling squares from different years. In future, we will therefore set up experiments with plants in pots, where we can tightly control the conditions, to check how high soil pH and salty soil affect grassland recovery.
